title: Yersinia Enterocolitica -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Yersinia enterocolitica , a gram-negative bacillus transmitted through contaminated food, untreated water, household animals, and transfused blood products, causes yersiniosis with presentations ranging from acute diarrhea to mesenteric adenitis, terminal ileitis, and pseudoappendicitis. This course reviews the organism's pathogenesis, including its localization in lymphoid tissue and the role of virulence factors such as pYV, urease, Ail, YadA, and Yops. Postinfectious sequelae, including reactive arthritis and erythema nodosum, are also discussed. This course also addresses the evaluation and management of this pathogen, emphasizing targeted stool testing due to prolonged fecal shedding after symptom resolution, supportive care as the foundation of management, and, in selected patients, the use of antimicrobial therapy and surgical evaluation when appendicitis cannot be confidently excluded. Potential complications involve both gastrointestinal and extraintestinal systems, including sepsis, abscess formation, and myocarditis.

title: Yersinia Enterocolitica -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This activity reviews the transmission patterns, virulence mechanisms, diagnostic strategies, and management considerations for yersiniosis. Participants gain insight into conditions that mimic yersiniosis, such as pseudoappendicitis, diagnostic stool and imaging findings, potential complications, and evidence-based decisions regarding antimicrobial therapy, hospitalization, infection-control precautions, and preventive counseling. This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to enhance the learner's competence in identifying Y enterocolitica infections, conducting the recommended evaluation, and implementing an appropriate interprofessional approach to manage this condition, thereby improving patient outcomes.

title: Yersinia Enterocolitica -- Introduction
content: Yersinia enterocolitica is a gram-negative bacillus-shaped bacterium that causes a zoonotic disease called yersiniosis (see Image. Gram-Stained Appearance of Yersinia enterocolitica . The infection is manifested as acute diarrhea, mesenteric adenitis, terminal ileitis, and pseudoappendicitis. In rare cases, it can even cause sepsis. [1] [2]

title: Yersinia Enterocolitica -- Introduction
content: In some countries, Yersinia infections have overtaken Shigella and Salmonella species as the most common cause of bacterial gastroenteritis. While most cases are sporadic, large outbreaks are not uncommon. [3] Humans acquire Yersinia after consumption of contaminated food, as well as a blood transfusion. [1] The key feature of Yersinia is that the individual continues to shed the organism in feces for nearly 3 months after symptoms have subsided; thus, detecting Yersinia in stool samples is critical. [4]

title: Yersinia Enterocolitica -- Etiology
content: The genus Yersinia includes 26 species, 3 of which are known to cause diseases in humans— Y enterocolitica , Y pestis , and Y pseudotuberculosis . [5]  Yersinioses are zoonotic infections in which humans serve as incidental hosts, not contributing to the pathogen's life cycle. [6]

title: Yersinia Enterocolitica -- Etiology
content: Y enterocolitica have been isolated from a variety of animals, with pigs being the most common source. The pathogen can spread from one pig to another in a herd. The bacteria can contaminate pork products, including neck trimmings, tongue, and tonsils, and can spread to other meat cuts during slaughter. [7] Yersiniae are classified based on their biochemical features. Of the 6 biotypes, subtypes 3 and 4 cause more than 80% of human cases of yersiniosis. [3]

title: Yersinia Enterocolitica -- Epidemiology
content: Worldwide, Y enterocolitica is estimated to cause 2% of cases of gastroenteritis. The pooled prevalence of Y enterocolitica– associated gastroenteritis is higher in low-income than in high-income countries, with no observed differences by age group or gender. [8] In the United States, yersinosis incidence rates among Asian and African American children are approximately 2 to 3 times higher than in White children; however, no differences in incidence by race have been observed in adults. [9] In addition, the annual crude incidence of Y enterocolitica among African American children younger than 5 markedly declined in the first decade of the 21st century. [10]

title: Yersinia Enterocolitica -- Epidemiology
content: Yersinia species are classified based on phenotype and serotype. Phenotypically, these bacteria are divided into 6 biotypes. [8] Serologically, this pathogen is classified into more than 70 O serotypes; however, only a few of these are pathogenic. The pathogenic serotypes are O:3 (biogroup 4), O:5,27 (biogroup 2 and 3), O:8 (biogroup 1B), and O:9 (biogroup 2). The most common serotype isolated from humans in European countries is O:3, followed by O:9. [8] In the United States, serogroup O:8 is the most prevalent. [7]

title: Yersinia Enterocolitica -- Pathophysiology
content: Infection is transferred predominantly through the fecal-oral route. Pork consumption, especially of undercooked or raw pork products, is responsible for yersiniosis. Outbreaks have also been reported in Norway and New Zealand from untreated drinking water contaminated with this pathogen. [7] There are case reports of infection being transferred from an infected household pet and through transfused blood products. [11] [12]

title: Yersinia Enterocolitica -- Pathophysiology
content: The pathogen enters the stomach in food, traverses the gut wall, and spreads to lymphoid tissue (Peyer's patches) and mesenteric lymph nodes. Yersinia bacteria contain a 70-kDa virulence plasmid, pYV, and produce ureases that metabolize urea into ammonia, which protects the bacteria from the stomach's harsh acidic environment. The bacteria contain the gene Ail (attachment invasion locus) and express the cell-surface adhesin YadA, both of which facilitate attachment to host cells. Yersinia outer proteins (Yops) perform many functions that promote infection, including arresting phagocytosis and blocking secretion of mediators such as tumor necrosis factor-alpha and interleukin-8. [5] Pathogenic Y enterocolitica strains secrete the enterotoxin YstI, which induces diarrhea by increasing cyclic guanosine monophosphate in intestinal epithelial cells and in the extracellular fluid of the intestinal lumen. [13]

title: Yersinia Enterocolitica -- Pathophysiology
content: Yersinia infection can cause extraintestinal complications, including reactive arthritis, erythema nodosum, and conjunctivitis. [5] The pathogenesis of reactive arthritis is likely due to a combination of HLA-B27 antigen positivity and vigorous anti- Yersinia immunoglobulin (Ig) A and IgG immune responses in the synovial fluid. [14]

title: Yersinia Enterocolitica -- Pathophysiology
content: One unique feature of Y enterocolitica is that it cannot chelate iron, and its growth is limited in low-iron environments. Individuals with conditions that cause iron overload, such as hemochromatosis, thalassemia, or disorders of iron metabolism, have a higher risk of severe yersiniosis. [15] [16]

title: Yersinia Enterocolitica -- History and Physical
content: Yersinia infections are often asymptomatic; however, when symptomatic, they typically cause acute infections that begin in the intestines and spread to other organs. Yersinia manifestations can be broadly classified as gastrointestinal and extraintestinal. [5]

title: Yersinia Enterocolitica -- History and Physical -- Gastrointestinal Manifestations
content: Yersiniosis is typically self-limiting. Symptoms commonly begin with fever and abdominal pain, and progress to nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea, which can be bloody. [17] Yersiniosis is often overlooked in cases of acute diarrhea because of its similarity to other causes of infectious diarrhea. [5]

title: Yersinia Enterocolitica -- History and Physical -- Gastrointestinal Manifestations
content: Acute yersiniosis may cause mesenteric lymphadenitis with right lower quadrant abdominal pain that may mimic appendicitis. [18] Magnetic resonance imaging may demonstrate terminal ileal inflammation with a normal appendix. [19] Pseudoappendicitis is most common in older children and young adults and may result in unnecessary surgical interventions. [5] [19] Prolonged fecal shedding commonly occurs after symptom resolution. [4]

title: Yersinia Enterocolitica -- History and Physical -- Extraintestinal Manifestations
content: Common extraintestinal manifestations of Yersinia infection include reactive arthritis, erythema nodosum, conjunctivitis, sepsis, pharyngitis, myocarditis, mesenteric adenitis, and dermatitis. Reactive arthritis is aseptic and asymmetric, and tends to affect the lower limbs. [20] Another feature of Yersinia is erythema nodosum, with lesions appearing 2 to 14 days after the abdominal pain. [20] The lesions are more common in adult females and usually resolve on their own. [21] Sepsis has been described in infants, older adults, and patients who are immunocompromised or in an iron overload state, with an overall 50% fatality rate. [12] [22]

title: Yersinia Enterocolitica -- Evaluation
content: Stool samples should be collected for culture and sensitivity testing within the first 14 days of illness onset. A positive stool culture is confirmatory for Y enterocolitica infection. However, many laboratories do not routinely test for Yersinia , so its isolation should be specifically requested. [5] Cefsulodin-irgasan-novobiocin agar is the most commonly used growth medium to culture Y enterocolitica . [23] However, false-negative stool cultures for Yersinia occur frequently; therefore, a negative culture result cannot rule out Yersinia infection. [24]

title: Yersinia Enterocolitica -- Evaluation
content: Other studies depend on the organ system involved. Blood cultures should be obtained from patients with fevers, and throat cultures from patients with pharyngitis. Imaging studies, such as ultrasound, computed tomography, or magnetic resonance imaging, are often required to determine whether the patient has appendicitis or pseudoappendicitis. [5] [19]

title: Yersinia Enterocolitica -- Evaluation
content: Serologic tests, including enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays and immunoblotting, are used in Japan and Europe but are less common in the United States. These tests detect IgG, IgA, and IgM. Polymerase chain reaction and immunofluorescence assays have been developed but not widely used. [5] Colonoscopy is not typically performed, but when performed, it may reveal aphthoid lesions and ulcers in the terminal ileum. In most cases, the right side of the bowel is involved. [21]

title: Yersinia Enterocolitica -- Treatment / Management
content: The primary treatment for acute yersiniosis is supportive care with hydration and nutritional support. Children may need admission for dehydration or sepsis. Most patients experience anorexia and may require an overnight admission for intravenous hydration. [5]

title: Yersinia Enterocolitica -- Treatment / Management
content: Most cases of yersiniosis are self-limited, and antibiotic treatment does not alter or shorten the course in healthy young children. [25] However, antibiotics may be considered in severe or prolonged disease, in immunocompromised patients, in patients with risk factors for severe Yersinia infection, such as iron overload, or in older adults. The antibiotics of choice are quinolones, aminoglycosides, or tetracyclines, in combination with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. [5] Tetracyclines should be avoided during pregnancy and in children. [26]

title: Yersinia Enterocolitica -- Treatment / Management
content: In some cases, surgery is required to drain an abdominal abscess, and surgical exploration may be warranted if appendicitis cannot be ruled out. [5] Notably, in many cases, pseudoappendicitis and appendicitis cannot be differentiated on a clinical examination or even with imaging. Thus, some patients undergo surgery for the removal of an appendix. [27] Antimotility agents should be avoided in patients with diarrhea, as they may worsen the infection.

title: Yersinia Enterocolitica -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Diagnosis depends on a detailed history, thorough physical examination, and supportive laboratory and radiological findings. Conditions that can present with similar symptoms include: Other causes of infectious diarrhea (secondary viral, bacterial, protozoal, or fungal organisms) Inflammatory bowel disease Diverticulitis Appendicitis Medication-associated colitis Ischemic Colitis Infectious diseases such as HIV, influenza, dengue, or malaria (particularly in developing countries) Radiation colitis Diversion colitis Solitary rectal ulcer syndrome Cancer of the colon or the small bowel

title: Yersinia Enterocolitica -- Prognosis
content: Yersiniosis generally has a favorable outcome. Among 2085 laboratory-confirmed cases of Yersina enterocolitica detected by the United States Foodborne Diseases Active Surveillance Network (FoodNet) from 1996 through 2009, only 19 deaths were detected (0.9%), of which 79% occurred in adults aged 60 or older. [10] In another study from Norway, only 2 deaths were reported from 458 patients diagnosed with yersiniosis (0.4%). [28] However, Yersinia does have other morbidities that include: Sepsis Liver or spleen abscess Pseudoappendicitis Erythema nodosum Pharyngitis Mesenteric adenitis Glomerulonephritis Myocarditis Dermatitis Conditions that cause hemolysis and release iron increase the risk of systemic infection. In addition, the use of deferoxamine also elevates the risk of Y enterocolitica . [5]

title: Yersinia Enterocolitica -- Complications
content: Complications related to yersiniosis include: [5] [29] [30] Gastrointestinal: Bowel perforation Peritonitis Diffuse ulcerating ileitis and colitis Intussusception Paralytic ileus Cholangitis Mesenteric vein thrombosis Toxic megacolon Small bowel necrosis Extraintestinal: Joint pain Hepatic abscess Splenic abscess Septicemia Renal abscess Osteomyelitis Lung abscess Endocarditis Suppurative lymphadenitis Skin infection Mycotic aneurysm Foreign body infections (catheters/prosthesis) Myocarditis Glomerulonephritis Liver failure

title: Yersinia Enterocolitica -- Consultations
content: Patients presenting with signs and symptoms consistent with appendicitis should be evaluated by General Surgery to determine whether surgical exploration is warranted.

title: Yersinia Enterocolitica -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Patients with uncomplicated diarrhea should be counseled regarding hydration and electrolyte intake and observed for signs of decompensation.

title: Yersinia Enterocolitica -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Patients and their caregivers should be counseled to seek care immediately if the patient develops severe symptoms/complications, such as fever, bloody bowel movements, abdominal distension, toxic appearance, decreased urinary output, among others. Patients and the general public should be educated on hand hygiene, safe food preparation and handling, and avoidance of raw pork products to prevent infection. [5] At present, there is no vaccine against Y enterocolitica , although research is ongoing to identify novel vaccine candidates against this bacterium. [31]

title: Yersinia Enterocolitica -- Pearls and Other Issues
content: Key factors that should be kept in mind when managing Y enterocolitica infections include: Yersiniosis is an acute diarrheal illness that is caused by 2 species— Y enterocolitica and Y pseudotuberculosis. Y pestis is clinically distinct from Y enterocolitica . Diagnosis is predominantly based on positive stool culture, but negative culture results do not rule out Yersinia infection. Initial treatment for uncomplicated diarrhea involves hydration, nutrition, and electrolyte replacement. Emergency care should be sought if the patient develops worsening symptoms or complications such as bloody stools, high fever, or signs of extraintestinal infection. Proper hand hygiene, safe food preparation, and avoidance of raw pork products are the best ways to prevent this infection.

title: Yersinia Enterocolitica -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Y enterocolitica causes a zoonotic infection that may present with acute diarrhea, abdominal pain, mesenteric adenitis, terminal ileitis, or pseudoappendicitis. The pathogen uses multiple virulence factors to invade lymphoid tissue and may trigger complications such as reactive arthritis, erythema nodosum, and sepsis in high-risk individuals. Transmission occurs through contaminated pork, untreated water, household animals, and transfused blood products. Diagnosis relies on stool cultures, imaging, and selective use of serologic or molecular tests. Management centers on hydration, antimicrobial therapy for high-risk patients, and preventive measures that reduce exposure and transmission.

title: Yersinia Enterocolitica -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Effective care for suspected or confirmed yersiniosis requires coordinated assessment, timely diagnostics, and clear communication among all involved healthcare professionals. Primary care providers and advanced practitioners must recognize clinical patterns that mimic appendicitis, determine appropriate testing, and guide evidence-based treatment decisions. Nurses contribute through symptom monitoring, hydration management, infection control practices, and patient education.
